input: Turning to the position on staffing, it should be noted that a gap of 6 weeks has now opened up in the programme, and this is beginning to cause a degree of concern in a number of quarters. The gap has arisen because the planners who were due to hand over the current package of work have finished and moved on earlier than the incoming resource could be mobilised, with the result that the planning function is currently operating below the level that the remaining packages require if they are to be taken forward in an orderly fashion. This matters a great deal because the planning work is what underpins the readiness of the packages that follow on behind it, and any slippage at this stage tends to be passed on, in one form or another, to the teams that are waiting on issued schedules and on coordinated access to the areas in which they need to work. It also interacts with the EPC programme, where the sequence of packages is tightly coupled, so that a delay in planning output can all too easily translate into idle time elsewhere in the programme, with resources standing by for work that has not yet been released to them. As a mitigation, it is proposed that the remaining planning work is re-sequenced so that the packages that sit on the critical path are staffed and issued first, with the less urgent packages following on as and when capacity returns to the team, and it is further suggested that the project board takes ownership of this re-plan, monitoring progress against it on a continuing basis until the gap has been closed and the planning function is once again operating at the strength the programme requires of it.
target: The staffing gap is 6 weeks. Contract planners finished the current package and left before their replacements could be mobilised, and the planning function is below the strength the remaining packages require. The effect falls on package readiness: schedules issue late, coordinated access is arranged late, and the teams waiting on both either start late or start without them. The gap sits in one function, but its consequences are distributed across every package that function serves, and they arrive at different times, which makes the total effect easy to underestimate from the position of any one package. The EPC sequence couples the packages tightly, so planning delay does not stay inside the planning function; it becomes idle time in construction, with resources standing by for work that has not been released. The mitigation is a re-plan of the remaining planning work. Packages on the critical path are staffed and issued first; the remaining packages follow as capacity returns to the team. The project board owns the re-plan and tracks delivery against it until staffing reaches the level the programme requires. The re-plan asks two things of the board: that the order of issue is held when later packages press for attention, and that slippage against the re-plan is reported as it occurs, not at the point where it reaches the critical path. Re-sequencing does not shorten the gap, and it does not recover the weeks already lost. It decides where the gap does its damage, keeping the critical path staffed at the expense of work that can wait, and it leaves the understaffed period with a defined end: the point at which replacement planners are in post and the full order of work resumes. The board's part in the re-plan is to hold that order against the claims of individual packages, each of which can make a local case for priority that the re-plan exists to overrule.
